records.title: Canada’s Mission with the New U.S. Congress
records.excerpt: Canada’s Mission with the New U.S. Congress - Policy Magazine About Us ADVERTISE Archive Search Canada’s Mission with the New U.S. Congress November 27, 2026 | In Policy Special | By Colin Robertson By Colin Robertson November 27, 2026 Adapted from testimony before the Standing Senate Committee on Foreign Affairs and International Trade, November 26, 2026. Canadian enterprises — from major manufacturers to mid-sized companies to small businesses — cannot thrive amid uncertainty. The question for Canadian diplomacy is whether American policy makers understand that, on this overarching point, we have a mutual interest. In our consulates in New York and Los Angeles, and later when I led the Advocacy Secretariat at our embassy in Washington, I learned what gets a legislator’s attention. Name a business in their district. Mention what it makes, who its Canadian customers are, and the names of the voters whose shifts depend on those orders. Better still, let the American who signs the paycheques do the talking. Consider the humble blueberry box. Maine’s wild blueberry growers use Canadian harvesting boxes that fit their processing equipment. When Donald Trump’s tariffs caught the boxes, Republican Senator Susan Collins got an earful from constituents. She pressed the administration for exemptions and got them. A grower facing the expense of replacing working equipment had an argument no Canadian diplomat could improve upon. Americans get the link to affordability. Americans feel the squeeze. In a November 20–23 Economist/YouGov poll , 28 per cent said price increases had affected their Thanksgiving plans. Asked separately about tariffs on imports, 49 per cent wanted them lowered. Only 13 per cent wanted them raised. Anti-tariff attitudes give us an opening. It takes a local customer to explain how much per year a Canadian product saves an American family. We have people to call in January: more than100 new House members, 19 incoming senators, and 21 new governors. Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon wrote to 59 governors and senators . His letter to Texas Senator-elect James Talarico put a dollar figure on Quebec–Texas trade and offered an introduction to Quebec’s delegation in Houston. With nine offices in the US, Quebec sets the bar for promoting the interests of la belle province , complementing the work of our consulates. Our objective is to be tariff-free and, if not, to make any tariffs as low as possible while renewing CUSMA for a full sixteen years, with one rulebook for what the three countries make together. The other premiers can learn from the Quebec approach starting with their own letter outlining their provincial-state inventory of interests and follow up with trade missions. Start the advocacy with the inaugurations of border-state governors. As Consul General in California, I attended Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger’s inauguration. There, I met his incoming trade advisors and continued my ongoing conversations with former Secretary of State George Schultz, a good friend of Canada. Alaska’s Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is inaugurated in December. The January calendar takes us to Michigan for Jocelyn Benson, Minnesota for Amy Klobuchar, Maine for Hannah Pingree and Ohio for Amy Acton. Lake Erie gives Ohio a border with Ontario and its manufacturers plenty to discuss. On each trip, invite the governor’s trade adviser to visit an employer who buys from Canada. Canadian parliamentarians can also help open doors that diplomats cannot. When I served in Washington, Senator Colin Kenny got me into Justice John Roberts’ confirmation hearing. Senator Jerry Grafstein introduced me to the Senate president pro tempore. Parliamentarians can keep those ties alive and expand them by visiting Washington. Provincial legislators can participate in regular meetings of regional state governments. Premiers are welcomed at governors meetings embracing the West, Great Lakes and New England. In my experience, American legislators will always raise defence issues. The Pentagon’s recent fact sheet takes Canada to task over military spending and the F-35 review. Canada has reached NATO’s two per cent of GDP benchmark and committed to significant investment in the High North. Our Arctic over-the-horizon radar project will give both countries earlier warning of threats. It is fair for Washington to ask whether our equipment will work with theirs but what Canada buys is Canada’s business. I’m reminded of Pierre Trudeau’s word for the Pentagon critics of his 1983 peace initiative. He called them “pipsqueaks.” The next CUSMA deadline is January 12 , when written submissions close for Washington’s 2027 CUSMA review. Having helped negotiate Canada-U.S. free trade and NAFTA, I would pair every Canadian supplier making a submission with an American customer. Invite Mexican partners to do likewise. Our objective is to be tariff-free and, if not, to make any tariffs as low as possible while renewing CUSMA for a full sixteen years, with one rulebook for what the three countries make together. For now, we need to help Canadian firms across Canada find their next customer overseas. A toolmaker in Windsor with a second market can ride out a bad month in Michigan and still be there when orders pick up. And will the Michigan company pick up the phone and tell their member of Congress why that Canadian toolmaker matters? Using advocacy at different levels, employing various voices, we can help ensure they make that call. records.title: Mexico Seeks US Talks on SpaceX Airspace Use as FAA Studies 456 Starbase Launches Per Year
records.excerpt: Title: Mexico Seeks US Talks on SpaceX Airspace Use as FAA Studies 456 Starbase Launches Per Year URL Source: http://www.techtimes.com/articles/331726/20261127/mexico-seeks-us-talks-spacex-airspace-use-faa-studies-456-starbase-launches-per-year.htm Final URL: https://www.techtimes.com/articles/331726/20261127/mexico-seeks-us-talks-spacex-airspace-use-faa-studies-456-starbase-launches-per-year.htm Published Time: 2026-11-27T21:30:34-05:00 Markdown Content: ![Image 1: SpaceX Launch Site](https://d.techtimes.com/en/full/479360/spacex-launch-site.jpg?w=836&f=1314dc35e36317c37cc07591f9d4936b) SpaceX/Unsplash.com Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum [said Thursday, Nov. 26](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/mexico-seeks-us-talks-about-suspected-spacex-debris), that her government is asking the United States, through its embassy, for a meeting on permission to use Mexican airspace for SpaceX launches, how often that use would be allowed and, "if necessary," relocating the Starbase launch site. The request is about flight paths as much as debris: Mexico's own air navigation service [logged Starship's upper stage](https://tiempo.com.mx/local/paso-de-starship-no-represento-riesgo-en-espacio-mexicano-sict/) inside Mexican airspace for seven minutes on Nov. 14, and the FAA is now [studying up to 456 launches](https://www.faa.gov/space/stakeholder_engagement/spacex_starship) a year at Starbase, more than 18 times the current 25-launch limit. The meeting has no date. According to [Al Jazeera's report](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/26/mexico-seeks-us-talks-about-suspected-spacex-debris), the U.S. Embassy referred questions to the State Department, which did not immediately respond, and SpaceX did not immediately comment. Sheinbaum described SpaceX as a private company whose operations affect national airspace and said the matter belongs with the U.S. government, [Mexico News Daily reported](https://mexiconewsdaily.com/news/sheinbaum-press-us-spacex-launches-after-starship-debris-hits-tamaulipas-beaches/). ### Starship's Nov. 14 Return Crossed Mexican Airspace for Seven Minutes Mexico's air navigation service, SENEAM, and its civil aviation agency, AFAC, reported that Starship [entered Mexican airspace at 3:08 p.m.](https://tiempo.com.mx/local/paso-de-starship-no-represento-riesgo-en-espacio-mexicano-sict/) Mexico City time (4:08 p.m. ET) on Nov. 14 and left seven minutes later. Mexico's transport ministry, SICT, said the crossing posed no risk to air operations. The agencies had [received an FAA notification](https://planoinformativo.com/1181904/spacex-podria-provocar-cambios-en-vuelos-de-mexico-este-sabado-por-regreso-de-nave-starship) the day before, on Nov. 13. At that point they described a crossing as only a possibility of about 15 minutes, and said they might coordinate route and schedule changes with airlines if it happened. ### Hazard-Area Notices Already Close Mexican Airspace for Starship Launches Launches close airspace too. For Starship Flight 13 on July 24, Mexico [published a notice to airmen](https://ops.group/blog/spacex-starship-launches-major-airspace-disruption/), NOTAM B1467/26, that defined a "dangerous area" of 14 coordinate points from the surface to unlimited altitude. The airline-operations group OPSGROUP reported that a medevac jet from Guatemala City was turned back near the Belize-Mexico border because the airspace ahead had closed. An [FAA letter of agreement](https://www.fastcompany.com/91552379/spacexs-rockets-are-creating-a-new-air-traffic-headache-for-the-faa) for Boca Chica launches names Mexico as a party and references Mexican air navigation officials, Fast Company reported in June after obtaining the documents. Kelvin Coleman, a former FAA director of the commercial space office, told the outlet that Mexico is included when flights are expected to pass through its airspace. FAA environmental reviews say some Starship launches during busy periods could disrupt as many as 200 flights per hour, and that southerly trajectories could [affect the airspace of Mexico](https://www.faa.gov/space/stakeholder_engagement/spacex_starship/SPANISH_FONSI_ROD_Add_Launch_Traj_Starship_RTLS_mission_profiles_SpaceX_Boca_Chica.pdf), Cuba, Jamaica and the Cayman Islands. ### Can Mexico Require Permission for Starship Flights Through Its Airspace? The law is unsettled where it matters most. The 1944 Chicago Convention gives every state ["complete and exclusive sovereignty"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_on_International_Civil_Aviation) over airspace above its territory, but there is [no international agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airspace) on how high that airspace reaches. Most countries use the Kármán line, 100 km (62 miles), as the boundary with outer space, and descending Space Shuttles flew closer than 80 km (50 miles) over other nations without first requesting permission. Space treaties point to the launching state. Under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, [private companies need authorization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Space_Treaty) and continuing supervision from their home state, and the launching state is liable for damage its space objects cause. Mexico and the United States have both [ratified the treaty](https://olemiss.edu/airandspacelaw/space-signatories/). Article IX lets a state [request a consultation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Space_Treaty) when it expects harmful interference from another state's activity. The 1972 Liability Convention, also ratified by both countries, makes a launching state [absolutely liable for damage](https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/liability-convention.html) on Earth's surface or to aircraft in flight, but [only states can bring claims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Liability_Convention), and the best-known claim was Canada's over the Soviet Cosmos 954 satellite in 1978. The convention [defines damage as loss of life](https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/liability-convention.html), personal injury, or loss of or damage to property, which leaves open how beach contamination would be treated. Mexico's request fits the consultation-and-diplomacy route; the reports reviewed do not identify any legal authority Mexico would invoke to force a move of a site on U.S. soil under a U.S. license. ### FAA Notice Studies 456 Launches Per Year and Never Mentions Mexico The FAA [published its notice of intent](https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2026-20963.pdf) for a programmatic environmental impact statement on Oct. 14. Phase 1 would allow up to 100 launches and 200 landings a year on any day. Phase 2 would allow up to 456 launches, restricted to weekdays, and 912 landings, "implemented within several years," against a current authorization of 25 launches and 50 landings. For analysis, the FAA assumes half of launches and landings occur between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m., with launch azimuths from 40 to 115 degrees. The 456 figure is a [ceiling under study](https://www.faa.gov/space/stakeholder_engagement/spacex_starship), not an approval. The notice includes temporary airspace closures in the federal action but [does not mention Mexico](https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2026-20963.pdf) or foreign airspace. Sheinbaum cited [up to 400 flights per year](https://mexiconewsdaily.com/news/sheinbaum-press-us-spacex-launches-after-starship-debris-hits-tamaulipas-beaches/) and asked what that would imply for Mexican airspace. The comment deadline is listed differently by two official sources: the FAA's [project page lists Dec. 7](https://www.faa.gov/space/stakeholder_engagement/spacex_starship), while the [Federal Register notice gives Nov. 30](https://public-inspection.federalregister.gov/2026-20963.pdf). Check the docket before filing. ### Profepa Collected Fragments While SpaceX Disputes That They Are Its Own [Debris began reaching Playa Bagdad](https://www.poresto.com/mexico/2026/11/17/mexico-recolecta-desecho

records.title: Fed rate hike odds rise to almost 100%: can AI selloff force a rethink?
records.excerpt: Markets are pricing in a near-certain probability of the Federal Reserve raising interest rates for the second time in three months at its December meeting.CME FedWatch data on Thursday showed a 99.4% probability of a rate hike in December, which would take the federal funds rate to the 4%-4.25% ra… Fed rate hike odds rise to almost 100%: can AI selloff force a rethink? 4 min read NDX Markets are pricing in a near-certain probability of the Federal Reserve raising interest rates for the second time in three months at its December meeting. CME FedWatch data on Thursday showed a 99.4% probability of a rate hike in December, which would take the federal funds rate to the 4%-4.25% range. The implied probability was around 97% a day earlier. Wednesday's inflation data appears to have essentially confirmed the expectations of another increase after the Kevin Warsh-led committee raised rates in September for the first time in three years. The latest figures have also raised questions about how much further borrowing costs may need to rise in 2027. However, the prospect of additional tightening comes at a difficult time for financial markets. A sharp selloff in artificial intelligence stocks has rattled Wall Street, with the Nasdaq 100 briefly entering bear-market territory on Wednesday, November 25, before recovering from its session lows. This has raised a difficult question for policymakers: could the deterioration in financial markets force the Fed to reconsider its tightening plans? Inflation data strengthen case for a hike The US personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.8% year over year in October, according to data released by the Commerce Department on Wednesday. Core PCE inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, increased to 3.3%, exceeding economists' expectations by 0.1 percentage point. Both measures remain considerably above the Fed's 2% inflation target, suggesting that price pressures have yet to return to levels policymakers consider acceptable. The latest figures followed October's consumer price index report, which showed headline inflation rising 0.4% on a monthly basis, compared with expectations of 0.3%. Core CPI increased 0.3%, matching the previous two months but exceeding the 0.2% forecast. Meanwhile, the US economy expanded at an annualised rate of 4.3% in the third quarter, according to the revised Commerce Department estimate. That was 0.9 percentage point higher than the initial estimate, reflecting stronger investment and consumer spending. The combination of persistent inflation and resilient economic growth gives policymakers little immediate reason to abandon their tightening approach. Williams reinforces Fed's inflation priority New York Fed President John Williams has also stressed that bringing inflation back to the central bank's target remains essential. Speaking at the University of Mount Saint Vincent in New York on November 23, Williams said inflation remained too high and that policymakers still had work to do. "But getting inflation back to 2% is 100% essential," he said. He also acknowledged that monetary policy cannot resolve supply-side disruptions directly, including problems affecting shipping routes, pipelines and refineries. However, he argued that the Fed must prevent such shocks from creating persistent inflationary pressures or weakening inflation expectations. Other Fed policymakers have also maintained similar views, suggesting that they are unlikely to tolerate elevated inflation simply because financial markets are struggling. Can AI selloff force Fed to reconsider? The growing turmoil in technology stocks has nevertheless introduced another consideration into the rate debate. The Nasdaq 100 briefly fell 20% below its October peak on Wednesday, meeting the definition of a bear market before recovering from its lows. Investors have been reducing exposure to AI-linked companies amid concerns about enormous infrastructure spending, expensive financing and uncertainty over whether the investments will generate sufficient returns. The Nvidia-Jensen Huang scandal regarding a suspected Chinese spy has also worried investors as the chipmaker and its star CEO remain central to the AI trade. Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, believes the market turmoil provides a strong argument for caution. "If they look at inflation, they should be hiking. But if you look at the outlook for AI, they should maybe be cutting," Slok told the Financial Times. He described the recent market turmoil as a very strong argument against aggressive rate increases. Claudia Sahm, chief economist at New Century Advisors, was less convinced that the selloff would change the Fed's immediate direction. "At this point, it's going to be hard to get them off this focus on inflation," she said to the Financial Times, adding that stock declines would need to become considerably larger to influence policymakers. A decline in equity prices can tighten financial conditions by making it more expensive for companies to raise capital and reducing household wealth. Bill Ackman warns against another rate hike Pershing Square founder Bill Ackman has been among the most vocal critics of the Fed's tightening approach. In a post on X, Ackman argued that financial conditions had already tightened substantially, pointing to rising borrowing costs and the recent decline in stock prices. He also questioned the central bank's 2% inflation target, arguing that geopolitical risks, tariffs, military expenditure and massive investments in AI infrastructure and energy have fundamentally changed the economic environment. Ackman believes a 3% inflation target would be more realistic under current circumstances. https://twitter.com/BillAckman/status/2124629409105944729 "The Fed will put the U.S. and world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%," he warned. For now, however, markets are overwhelmingly positioned for another increase. The December 8-9 meeting will test whether policymakers remain focused on persistent inflation or become concerned about the economic consequences of tighter financial conditions. records.title: Greer signals room for Canada in any change to U.S. auto and steel tariffs
records.excerpt: The article reports on comments from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer suggesting Canada could be included in potential adjustments to American auto and steel tariffs. With Donald Trump threatening to double U.S. tariffs on Canadian vehicles to 50 percent on Jan. 1, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Wednesday that any change to Washington’s sectoral duties would have to include something for Canada. Flavio Volpe, president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers’ Association, said the wording shows the talks need not be zero-sum, but warned that every point remains in dispute. Greer put conditions on the remark. Any new arrangement would first have to work for the United States, he said. He gave no sign of what Canada might get, or whether Washington will change the duties at all. Speaking to CNBC, he said American auto and steel production has recovered behind the tariffs. “We’re seeing a lot of resurgence in autos and steel. So the president wants to be careful about any potential modifications on that front, including with Canada,” he said. “We want to make sure that North American trade in these products is beneficial for the United States, obviously. There will have to be something that accommodates Canada as well, if there’s a change that’s made,” Greer told the network. The comments come as a stalemate grows more expensive. Under Section 232 of the U.S. Trade Expansion Act of 1962, Canadian-built vehicles face a 25 percent tariff, and steel and aluminum have faced 50 percent since June 2025. On Aug. 24, days after talks collapsed, Trump posted that tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks, auto parts and steel would rise to 50 percent on Jan. 1, 2027. Steel is already at that rate, so the increase falls mainly on autos. Separate 50 percent duties under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 took effect Aug. 22 on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods. The Bank of Canada warned in April that the sectoral tariffs were already hurting the Canadian economy. What an accommodation could look like The sectors in dispute haven’t changed. Greer said a conversation with Canadian officials last week left autos, steel and aluminum as the main sticking points, The Canadian Press reported. He did not say which duties might be eased, by how much, or in exchange for what. Global News, citing people briefed by the federal government, has reported that the 25 percent auto tariff is the biggest unresolved issue. According to The Hub ‘s reporting , the U.S. offered in August to cut that rate to 15 percent, with no carve-out for CUSMA-compliant vehicles. Volpe, who also sits on the Advisory Committee on Canada-U.S. Economic Relations, read the language as a diplomatic shift. Greer’s use of the word “accommodate” “helps negotiators understand that the objective isn’t zero sum,” Volpe told CTV News . Talks broke down on Aug. 21. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Washington had added last-minute demands that would restrict Canada’s ability to strike trade deals with other countries. Greer has said Canada walked away from a nearly finished agreement. The two sides have since re-engaged. On Sunday, Greer told Fox News they were “fairly close on finding a landing zone,” and Carney and Trump discussed trade in Shenzhen, China, last week. Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc has been more guarded. He told Radio-Canada that progress has been made but Canada is not on the verge of signing. Canada’s ties with China remain a sore point. Greer criticized Ottawa’s tariff cuts on Chinese electric vehicles, steel and aluminum, saying the approach “goes a little bit backwards.” After the August breakdown, Greer told CBC News that lower U.S. barriers on steel, aluminum and cars would come with an expectation that partners also protect their borders. Canadian negotiators had hoped a so-called fortress North America would mean no tariffs inside it and agreed tariffs on those outside, The Hub reported . As that piece noted, CUSMA’s Article 32.10 already requires Canada to give the U.S. three months’ notice before starting free trade talks with a “non-market” country. LeBlanc said in Ottawa that Greer called him over the weekend about a separate White House proposal to raise tariffs on 12 countries, the European Union and Taiwan, aimed at subsidized manufacturing and overproduction. Canada is not on the list. LeBlanc said his team is studying the measures and that he expects talks to resume next week, after American Thanksgiving. Doubts about the tariffs’ payoff Greer offered no figures to support his account of a U.S. manufacturing revival, and the research on steel tariffs gives reason for doubt. Economists James Lake and Ding Liu examined President George W. Bush’s 2002 steel safeguard tariffs across U.S. local labour markets in a study published in November 2025 in the American Economic Journal: Economic Policy . They found the tariffs did nothing for steel employment. They did cut jobs in industries that use steel, and those losses lasted for years after the tariffs were lifted in December 2003. The damage was worst in places with lower education levels or a heavy reliance on steel-using manufacturing, and many plants that closed never reopened. Washington treats the sectoral tariffs as a success worth protecting, which could make them harder to unwind than Greer’s softer language suggests. Any accommodation depends on a change both sides have yet to agree on, and past offers to lower U.S. barriers have come with conditions on Canada’s trade with other countries. The clearest test is whether the auto increase goes ahead in January. Greer added that Trump and Carney will have several chances to meet before December’s G20 summit. Without a deal, Trump has said the higher rate will take effect Jan. 1, 2027. The Hub Staff The Hub’s mission is to create and curate news, analysis, and insights about a dynamic and better future for Canada in a… U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer indicated that any changes to U.S. tariffs on Canadian vehicles and steel must include considerations for Canada. With President Trump threatening to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles to 50% starting January 1, 2027, Greer emphasized that any new arrangement must first benefit the U.S. and hinted at the need for accommodations for Canada. The ongoing trade negotiations remain complex, with unresolved issues primarily surrounding auto tariffs. Canadian officials have expressed concerns about the impact of these tariffs on the Canadian economy, as discussions continue between U.S. and Canadian leaders. Canadian-built vehicles face a 25 percent tariff under Section 232. Steel and aluminum have faced 50 percent tariffs since June 2025. records.excerpt: A roughly 10% weekly drop followed by a sharp bounce is the kind of whiplash that tends to linger. One options-based ETF is designed for it. Free Article Explore Premium Services History Says the Nasdaq's Wild Ride Probably Isn't Over. Here's the Case for QQQI and Its 14% Yield. A roughly 10% weekly drop followed by a sharp bounce is the kind of whiplash that tends to linger. One options-based ETF is designed for it. By David Dierking – Nov 27, 2026 at 5:48PM EST Key Points The Nasdaq-100 lost about 10% last week and bounced hard on Monday, a pattern history says rarely settles quickly. QQQI sells and buys options on the index, which tends to help when markets go sideways. QQQI will likely trail in a steady rebound and offers little cushion in a straight drop. 10 stocks we like better than Neos ETF Trust - Neos Nasdaq-100 High Income ETF › Last week, the Nasdaq-100 fell more than 10% on the week, and briefly touched bear market territory, falling 20% below its October high. On Monday, it rebounded roughly 7% after Nvidia 's ( NVDA +0.80% ) board brought back co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO. A bounce that large may feel like the bottom is in. But right now, volatility is still too high to comfortably say which direction the market is headed next. One alternative to owning the Nasdaq-100 here is the NEOS Nasdaq-100 High Income ETF ( QQQI +2.60% ) . Its covered call strategy and 14% distribution yield could be a compelling option for taking some tech-sector risk off the table. Image source: Getty Images. Big weekly drops tend to bring more big swings The week ending last Friday was only the 13th weekly loss of 10% or more in the Nasdaq-100's history. The VIX, which is a measure of expected market volatility, briefly touched 40 for the first time since April 2025. But the CBOE's own research shows that when the equity market experiences a volatility shock, the residual volatility "may remain for weeks, months, and even years going forward." Since higher volatility is usually correlated with falling stock prices, the implication is that the downside may not be finished. QQQI - Neos ETF Trust - Neos Nasdaq-100 High Income ETF $48.59 +$1.23 (+2.60%) NASDAQ · As of 1:00 PM ET 11/27/26 Key data points AUM $14.17B Dividend yield 15.61% Expense ratio 0.68% Top holdings AAPL 9.17% MSFT 6.44% NVDA 6.34% Why QQQI can be a Nasdaq-100 alternative The NEOS Nasdaq-100 High Income ETF owns the stocks in the Nasdaq-100 index and then sells call options on the index, collecting premiums that usually increase when volatility rises. Unlike more traditional covered call strategies, the fund also buys some higher-priced calls. It does this to maintain some share price upside, which many covered call ETFs largely give up. The Nasdaq-100 is usually more volatile, so the yields generated by this fund also tend to run higher. As of Nov. 23, the distribution yield is 14.1%. Using the phrase "distribution yield" instead of dividend yield isn't an accident. The income comes from options premiums received, not dividends paid by corporations. Therefore, the tax treatment may differ. When investing in a covered call ETF, the trade-off is that you give up share price appreciation potential in exchange for the high yield. If you believe stocks will move sideways or lower, a fund like the NEOS Nasdaq-100 High Income ETF can outperform the Nasdaq-100. In a steady bull market, however, it's likely to lag. Given how stocks have already turned volatile, significant questions remain about AI capital expenditures, inflation is high, and the Federal Reserve may hike rates multiple times over the next several months, there's a clear case for why the high-yield strategy makes more sense right now. How to think about investing in QQQI Don't think of QQQI as getting a free 14% yield on top of investing in the Nasdaq-100. There's a clear trade-off, and one you need to consider first. Covered call strategies usually work best in sideways-trending, lower-volatility markets. They usually offer the best opportunity to beat the index while still generating positive total returns. The second best is downtrending markets. In this case, QQQI would capture most, if not all, of any loss in the Nasdaq-100, while the high yield would help offset some of it. In other words, you're probably losing less than the Nasdaq-100 but still outperforming. Given the market's history during sharp corrections and current macro conditions, I believe we're more likely in a longer-lasting, higher-volatility environment. That's not necessarily the best environment for total returns, but a covered call ETF could increase the chances of outperformance. Plus, option premiums tend to rise during periods of higher volatility, which improves overall yield. Overall, the NEOS Nasdaq-100 High Income ETF offers one of the best options in the high-yield covered call ETF space. It uses a fairly straightforward strategy, and the 14% yield is quite attractive. If volatility continues, I like this as a potential alternative to owning tech stocks outright. Where to invest $1,000 right now When our analyst team has a stock tip, it can pay to listen. records.excerpt: Title: S&P 500, Nasdaq, Dow Forecast: Wall Street Rebound Faces Major Resistance—Bull Trap or Breakout? URL Source: http://www.stonex.com/en-gb/news-and-analysis/sandp-500-nasdaq-dow-forecast-wall-street-rebound-faces-major-resistance-bull-trap-or-breakout/ Final URL: https://www.stonex.com/en-gb/news-and-analysis/sandp-500-nasdaq-dow-forecast-wall-street-rebound-faces-major-resistance-bull-trap-or-breakout/ Markdown Content: ## **Equity Indices Technical Forecast: Weekly Trade Levels** * S&P 500 rebounds from major support, with weekly momentum holding above its March lows. * Nasdaq remains vulnerable after breaking its 2025 uptrend, with former support now capping recovery attempts. * Dow Jones leads the recovery, but buyers have struggled to overcome the 52-week moving average. * A failure to defend last week's lows would renew pressure on the broader equity-market recovery. * Next week's ISM surveys and November employment report could fuel volatility as Fed policy expectations remain in focus. The U.S. equity markets are approaching the November monthly close at a critical technical crossroads following a volatile stretch that has significantly weakened the broader market structure. Despite the sharp recovery from last week's lows, the rebound has yet to establish a convincing shift in trend, leaving buyers facing an important challenge as December trade gets underway. Improving market participation offers some encouragement, although the divergence between major indices continues to highlight underlying vulnerabilities. With the recovery approaching key technical hurdles, the focus remains on whether bulls can build on the latest advance or whether renewed selling pressure will threaten another leg lower. ##### **S&P 500 — Sharp Recovery Highlights Improving Market Breadth** The S&P 500 staged an impressive recovery Wednesday after an early selloff threatened to extend the broader November decline. The index rebounded sharply from session lows as buyers returned across most sectors, with nearly three-quarters of its constituents trading higher despite continued weakness in heavily weighted technology shares. The divergence highlights an important shift in market dynamics, with improving breadth suggesting underlying demand remains more resilient than the headline index would indicate. The focus into Friday's abbreviated session and the November monthly close is on whether broader participation can sustain the recovery or whether persistent weakness in mega cap technology stocks will continue to limit upside. ##### **S&P 500 Price Chart – SPX500 Weekly** ![Image 1: image-20261125163711-5](https://micms.stonex.com//sites/default/files/inline-images/image-20261125163711-5.png) _Chart Prepared by Michael Boutros, Sr. Technical Strategist;_[_S&P 500 on TradingView_](https://www.tradingview.com/symbols/SPX500/?exchange=FOREXCOM) **Technical Outlook:** In last month’s [**S&P 500 Forecast**](https://www.stonex.com/en-gb/news-and-analysis/sandp-500-nasdaq-dow-forecast-nasdaq-selloff-deepens-as-dow-rally-stalls/) we noted that our focus was, “on a breakout of the October range for directional guidance into the close of the month- losses would need to be limited to 7482 to avert a larger correction within the broader uptrend.” The October range broke lower into the close of the month with the subsequent decline extending more than 12.2% off the record high. The decline broke below the median line of the 2025 pitchfork before rebounding off confluent support last week at the 61.8% retracement of the yearly range and the 2025 high-week close (HWC) at **6896-6929**. Weekly RSI has now defended the March lows in momentum, and the focus is on whether the bulls can build on this rebound into the close of the month. This week’s recovery has been capped by confluent resistance at **7246/58**- a region defined by the 52-week moving average, the 38.2% retracement of the October decline, and the 38.2% retracement of the yearly range. Key resistance is eyed at the 61.8% retracement at **7477** which converges on the median line next month, and a breach / weekly close above this threshold would be needed to suggest a more significant low is in place. Subsequent resistance is eyed at the May high close near **7578** and the August high-week close (HWC) / record high at**7781-7817**. A break below this week’s low would threaten a test of the 2025 uptrend with subsequent support seen at the February low at **6731** and **6500/65**- a region defined by the October / November lows and the 2026 low-week close (LWC). A weekly close below this threshold would be needed to validate a break of the uptrend and suggest a larger trend reversal is underway. **Bottom line:** The immediate focus is on a breakout of the 6896-7250 range for guidance with the bulls still vulnerable while below 7477. ##### **Nasdaq — Technology Rebound Faces a Critical Test** The Nasdaq remained at the center of this week's volatility, with Monday's explosive technology-led rally giving way to renewed selling before Wednesday's dramatic intraday recovery. Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO helped fuel Monday's surge, but the subsequent reversal in the shares highlights how fragile investor sentiment remains. records.title: Frontier Nuclear Receives Nasdaq Notification Regarding Minimum Bid Price Deficiency
records.excerpt: Winnipeg, Manitoba--(Newsfile Corp. - November 27, 2026) - Frontier Nuclear and Minerals Inc. NASDAQ:FNUC ("Frontier"), a nuclear fuel cycle company, announces that on November 25, 2026, it received a written notification letter (the "Notification Letter") from the Nasdaq Stock Market LLC ("Nasdaq"… Frontier Nuclear Receives Nasdaq Notification Regarding Minimum Bid Price Deficiency 4 min read FNUC Winnipeg, Manitoba--(Newsfile Corp. - November 27, 2026) - Frontier Nuclear and Minerals Inc. FNUC ("Frontier"), a nuclear fuel cycle company, announces that on November 25, 2026, it received a written notification letter (the "Notification Letter") from the Nasdaq Stock Market LLC ("Nasdaq"), notifying Frontier that it was not in compliance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2), as the minimum bid price of Frontier's common shares ("Shares") has been below US $1.00 per share for 30 consecutive business days. The Notification Letter is only a notification of deficiency and not a notice of delisting. As such, the Notification Letter has no immediate effect on the listing or trading of Frontier's Shares on the Nasdaq Capital Market under the symbol "FNUC." Nasdaq Listing Rules Nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2) requires securities listed on the Nasdaq Capital Market to maintain a minimum bid price of US$1.00 per share, and Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(A) provides that a failure to meet the minimum bid price requirement exists if the deficiency continues for a period of 30 consecutive business days. Based on the closing bid price of Frontier's Shares for the 30 consecutive business days from October 14, 2026 to November 24, 2026, Frontier has not met the minimum bid price requirement. In accordance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(A), Frontier has a period of 180 calendar days, or until May 24, 2027 in which to regain compliance with the minimum bid price requirement. To regain compliance, the closing bid price of the Frontier's Shares must meet or exceed US $1.00 for at least ten consecutive business days during this 180-calendar day period. In the event Frontier does not regain compliance by May 24, 2027, Frontier may be eligible for an additional 180 calendar day grace period if it meets the continued listing requirement for market value of publicly held shares (US $1 million) and all other initial listing standards for The Nasdaq Capital Market, with the exception of the bid price and provides written notice to Nasdaq of its intention to cure the deficiency during the second compliance period, by effecting a reverse stock split, if necessary. If it appears to Nasdaq that Frontier will not be able to cure the deficiency, or if Frontier is not otherwise eligible for additional time to regain compliance, Frontier's Shares will be subject to delisting by Nasdaq. Frontier may still appeal Nasdaq's determination to delist its Shares, and during any appeal process, Frontier's Shares would continue to trade on the Nasdaq Capital Market. Frontier is issuing this press release pursuant to Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(b). Nasdaq advised Frontier that it will be added to Nasdaq's public list of non-compliant companies beginning five business days after the date of the notice. Nasdaq will also distribute a non-compliance indicator through its market data network and make it available to third-party market data providers. Frontier's management intends to actively monitor the bid price for its Shares and will consider all available options to regain compliance with the Nasdaq minimum bid price requirement. Frontier's business operations are not affected by the receipt of the Notification Letter. About Frontier Nuclear and Minerals Inc. records.excerpt: US equity futures posted substantial gains on Friday, indicating a potential recovery for Wall Street following weeks of selling pressure across artificial i... Wall Street Futures Climb as Technology Stocks Rebound While AI Export Controls and Middle East Tensions Remain in Focus: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq Fiona Craig Fri, 27 November 2026 at 2:08 am GMT-8 5 min read ^NDX SPCX ^GSPC ^DJI Wall Street bull ©Shutterstock US equity futures posted substantial gains on Friday, indicating a potential recovery for Wall Street following weeks of selling pressure across artificial intelligence and other growth-oriented stocks. The improving market sentiment comes despite growing uncertainty surrounding Asian data centre financing following new US semiconductor export restrictions, alongside renewed security concerns affecting Middle Eastern oil infrastructure and shipping. Developments involving SpaceX share donations and rising US food prices are also drawing investor attention. Nasdaq 100 Futures Lead Gains Ahead of Shortened US Trading Session Technology stocks appeared positioned for a recovery on Friday as US equity futures advanced following significant declines during October and November. At approximately 08:49 GMT, Nasdaq 100 futures had risen 2.6% to 26,774 points. S&P 500 futures gained 1.95% to 7,323 points, while Dow Jones futures advanced 1.2% to 50,825 points. Market participation is expected to remain limited following the Thanksgiving holiday, with US exchanges scheduled to close early on Friday. Wednesday's trading session had already shown signs of stabilisation. The Nasdaq Composite recovered from losses of up to 4.5% during the session to finish 0.6% lower, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.25% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.3%. Gains across Asian and European technology stocks on Thursday provided further support for sentiment ahead of Wall Street's reopening. New AI Chip Rules Prompt Banks to Reassess Asian Data Centre Loans Financial institutions are reviewing billions of dollars in planned lending to Asian data centre operators following the introduction of tighter US controls on advanced artificial intelligence semiconductors, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday. According to people familiar with the matter cited in the report, concerns over regulatory compliance and exposure to Chinese technology companies have prompted some lenders to delay or withdraw from financing arrangements. Bridge Data Centres, owned by Bain Capital, is seeking an expanded $6.6 billion loan. The company operates Malaysian facilities serving customers including ByteDance, with lenders reportedly conducting additional due diligence before proceeding. Digital Halo, a Malaysian data centre operator backed by Partners Group, has also encountered financing uncertainty after one bank withdrew from a fully underwritten $372 million loan and other lenders raised additional questions. Meanwhile, banks are reconsidering a separate $480 million financing arrangement for Singapore-based cloud infrastructure provider Aolani, which also provides services to ByteDance. Under the new restrictions, companies operating in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil must obtain government licences to purchase advanced AI chips from US manufacturers. Additional licensing requirements apply to data centres worldwide that provide significant computing capacity to Chinese businesses, with operators given 90 days to obtain the necessary approvals to maintain those arrangements. SpaceX Share Donation Plans Raise Questions Over Implementation and Dilution Elon Musk has expanded his proposed SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) share donation initiative, announcing on Thursday that he intends to provide an additional share to every American child annually. The announcement follows an earlier pledge under which children would receive two shares, one from Musk's personal holdings and another from SpaceX. Musk indicated that the shares originating from his own holdings would be transferred once his lock-up restrictions expire in June 2027. SpaceX separately announced on Wednesday that it would allocate one newly issued Class A common share to every currently active Trump Account. Established in 2025, the accounts are intended to operate similarly to individual retirement savings accounts for US residents under the age of 18. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband previously announced plans in October to contribute part of their holdings to support more than two million children through the programme. The financial implications of the initiative will depend in part on the final eligibility requirements, allocation mechanisms and the extent of any new share issuance. Further details will be relevant to assessing potential dilution for existing shareholders. Retailers Cut Thanksgiving Meal Prices Despite Higher Grocery Costs US retailers are competing for holiday spending by offering discounted Thanksgiving meal packages, even as industry figures indicate that the average cost of a traditional dinner has increased. Walmart (NYSE:WMT) introduced a Thanksgiving meal package for 10 people priced at $35, compared with just under $40 last year. German discount supermarket chain Lidl initially priced its equivalent package at $35.86 before introducing a further $2 reduction. These promotional offers contrast with data from the American Farm Bureau Federation, which reported a 10% annual increase in the average price of a 16-pound frozen turkey to $23.86. Separate figures from Expana showed frozen turkey prices reaching a record $1.95 per pound, representing an increase of 9.6% since the beginning of 2026. The Farm Bureau estimated that the average cost of a Thanksgiving meal for 10 people reached $58.63 in 2026, up 6% from the previous year. The increase marks the first annual rise since 2022, when the average cost stood at $64.05. While promotional pricing may help retailers attract customers, persistent food inflation remains relevant to consumer purchasing power, discretionary spending and retail profit margins. Brent Heads for First Weekly Gain of November as Regional Supply Risks Persist Crude oil markets were mixed on Friday as renewed attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial vessels in the Middle East raised concerns about potential supply disruptions. Brent crude futures declined 0.1% to $96.51 a barrel at 04:15 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate futures gained 2.5% to $85.78 a barrel at 04:26 GMT. Despite the modest decline, Brent remained on course for a weekly increase of approximately 4.5%, its first weekly gain of November. However, the international benchmark was still trading nearly 20% lower for the month. Attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants have affected Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure, with some operations at the Jazan refinery temporarily disrupted. The incident followed an earlier attack targeting the Ras Tanura refinery and export facility. Saudi authorities confirmed that one Nepalese employee was killed and several others were injured in the Jazan incident. Regional tensions increased further following a fatal drone-related incident in Kuwait involving Italian nationals. Kuwait attributed responsibility to Iran, although Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi rejected the allegation. Maritime security concerns also remain elevated around the Strait of Hormuz. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported an incident involving a commercial tanker, while Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed separately that several vessels had encountered naval mines. The security situation across key energy production and transportation facilities remains a source of uncertainty for global crude oil markets. records.excerpt: S&P 500, Nasdaq and Dow set for winning week despite AI turbulence Subscribe Markets The S&P 500, Nasdaq and Dow are all on pace for winning weeks despite the AI turbulence Stock futures rose before Friday's 1 p.m. ET close, though AI stocks including Nvidia have given back some of Monday's gains By Cris Tolomia · 2 min read · Updated November 27, 2026 Add QZ to Google Michael M. Santiago / Getty Images The S&P 500, Nasdaq $NDAQ Composite and Dow Jones Industrial Average are on pace for weekly gains as U.S. stock futures rose ahead of Friday's holiday-shortened session. The S&P 500 has climbed close to 4% for the week, and both the Nasdaq and the Dow have advanced by over 4%. S&P 500 futures were up close to 2% on Friday, Nasdaq -100 futures advanced 2.8%, and Dow futures gained 655 points, or 1.3%. U.S. markets took Thursday off for Thanksgiving and will shut early on Friday, at 1 p.m. ET. The week opened with Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia $NVDA CEO, according to CNBC . Nvidia stock jumped 31% on Monday. According to CNBC, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq each had their best day since April 2025. The Dow climbed more than 1,400 points on Monday, a gain of 3%. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq have been squeezed since then, with Nvidia and other AI-linked shares surrendering a portion of Monday's advance. Overseas, Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.3%, South Korea's Kospi gained 0.6% and Australia's S&P/ASX 200 added 0.4%. Germany's DAX was up around 1%, the U.K.'s FTSE 100 rose 0.7% and France's CAC 40 gained 0.4%. Sentiment on AI-related bets was already subdued ahead of Huang's departure, according to CNBC. Investors were uneasy about debt financing, hints that capital outlays were cooling, and the prospect that data centers would be built more slowly after Democrats won in the midterms. "The hyperscalers ultimately have to get an ROI, and they ultimately need to rebuild their free cash flow," Richard Clode, a portfolio manager at Janus Henderson, told CNBC. He said capital spending will not be sustained unless companies such as Anthropic show they can generate the expected revenue growth. Some on Wall Street attribute the recent weakness more to the prospect of Federal Reserve rate increases than to AI worries, according to CNBC. The most recent reading of the personal consumption expenditures price index bolstered traders' bets on several increases in the months ahead. "Most of this stuff really comes down to the Fed. That's the intermediate term factor," Warren Pies, co-founder of 3Fourteen Research, told CNBC. He said a good number of those his firm talked to fear a "replay of 2018," when the central bank lifted rates on four occasions. After the strong rebound seen at the beginning of the week, when the index advanced nearly **6.0%** during Monday's session, the following two sessions ahead of the Thanksgiving market closure have reflected a decline of roughly **3.0%**, highlighting that uncertainty is once again becoming an important feature of the index's price action. Part of the confidence that had returned to the market thanks to **Nvidia** at the start of the week has begun to fade following recent announcements regarding potential tariffs from the United States. Added to this is the possibility of a more aggressive **Federal Reserve**, which continues to act as a constant source of uncertainty for markets. Together, these factors have once again complicated the recovery in sentiment and could continue highlighting a period of indecision around the **Nasdaq 100** in the short term. #### **Are Tariffs Returning?** Although the bullish move around the **Nasdaq 100** was quite significant at the start of the week due to the relief generated by **Jensen Huang's** return as president of **Nvidia**, that recovery in confidence failed to remain consistent. In fact, during today's session the index fell nearly **4.5%**, a move that now appears linked to a new source of uncertainty for risk assets: the recent announcements of potential tariffs from the United States. During the session, it became known that, following a trade investigation, the United States determined that at least **14 major economies**, including the **European Union** and **China**, maintain industrial policies that could distort global competition and negatively affect U.S. industry over the long term. As a result, proposals involving new import tariffs have once again emerged. Tariffs of up to **20%** are being considered for the European Union and China, while economies such as **Japan**, **South Korea**, and **Taiwan** could face tariffs of around **15%**. While these measures have not yet been implemented, the announcement has been enough to reintroduce concerns related to inflation, corporate margins, and global economic growth. Many companies continue to depend on international supply chains, and a potential escalation in trade tensions could increase costs and affect business activity over the coming months. This situation appears to have slowed the recovery in sentiment seen at the start of the week. In fact, indicators such as the **Fear & Greed Index** continue to hover around **16 points**, reflecting an **"extreme fear"** environment and highlighting that investors remain cautious as new risks emerge for economic growth. ![Image 1](https://micms.stonex.com//sites/default/files/inline-images-2/5882/FEARGREED1125.png) Source: CNN The situation is particularly relevant for the **Nasdaq 100**, given the significant exposure many of its companies have to global supply chains. This uncertainty has also been reflected in the performance of the index's largest components. Looking at the ten most influential companies within the Nasdaq, only **Apple (+0.3%)**, **SpaceX (+0.95%)**, and **Meta (+2.56%)** managed to post gains during the session, while the remaining components recorded notable declines, reflecting that confidence around the technology sector remains relatively fragile. ![Image 2](https://micms.stonex.com//sites/default/files/inline-images-2/5882/Nasdaqcomponents1125.png) Source: Slickcharts With all of this in mind, the boost in confidence generated by Nvidia earlier in the week appears to be losing momentum. The market is now facing a new source of uncertainty linked to the possibility of an escalation in trade tensions, a development that could affect the long-term outlook for companies. Until there is greater clarity regarding the direction these proposals will take, the current phase of indecision facing the **Nasdaq 100** could remain relevant over the coming weeks. #### **Is the Central Bank Still a Threat?** Another important factor to consider is that markets continue to price in a more aggressive **Federal Reserve** over the coming months. There is currently close to a **100% probability** that the Fed will raise rates again at the **December 9** meeting, taking the benchmark rate toward the **4.25%** area. This expectation remained intact even after the release of the latest **Core PCE Index YoY**, where inflationary pressures once again came in above expectations. Markets had expected a reading of **3.2%**, but the official figure reached **3.3%**, reinforcing the view that inflationary pressures remain relevant within the U.S. economy. This suggests that the conditions necessary for a more aggressive Federal Reserve remain in place. At the same time, a higher interest-rate environment could increase borrowing costs, affect consumer spending, and reduce liquidity available for risk assets such as Nasdaq. As a result, if new economic data or Fed commentary continue supporting a more aggressive central bank into year-end, indecision or even a new period of weakness could remain relevant around the **Nasdaq 100** over the coming weeks. #### **Nasdaq 100 Technical Forecast** ![Image 3](https://micms.stonex.com//sites/default/files/inline-images-2/5882/NAS100_2026-11-25_14-33-41.png) Source: StoneX, Tradingview * **Bearish trend remains in place:**Since the first days of October, the **Nasdaq 100** has been developing a pattern of progressively lower highs and lower lows. The decline observed over recent weeks has given this structure even greater relevance, breaking the trading range that had remained in place for months and giving way to a new bearish phase that currently stands out as the chart's dominant technical pattern. The recovery attempt seen at the beginning of the week was not enough to put this structure at risk, meaning it could remain an important reference for price action in the weeks ahead. * **MACD:** The **MACD** histogram continues to develop below the neutral **0** line, reflecting meaningful selling pressure around short-term moving averages. This suggests that, on average, selling momentum continues to dominate and could keep highlighting a bearish dynamic within the chart over the short term. **Key Levels:** * **26,600 points - Key Resistance:** This barrier corresponds to one of the most important retracement areas observed in previous weeks and also coincides with the base of the new bearish structure. records.excerpt: True North launches Canada Life Centre venue tours | Winnipeg Jets Skip to Main Content True North launches Canada Life Centre venue tours Fans’ backstage pass to the home of the Jets and Moose By True North Sports + Entertainment Press Release November 25, 2026 WINNIPEG, Nov. 25, 2026 – Fans can now experience Canada Life Centre like never before with the launch of its venue tour program. The 90-minute guided tour will provide exclusive access to behind-the-scenes spaces and offer a glimpse into day-to-day operations. For more than two decades, Canada Life Centre has been Manitoba’s leading stage for premier sports and the biggest names in entertainment. Venue and team history will come to life through insider stories and a closer look at the details and features that make the home of the Winnipeg Jets and Manitoba Moose unique. Highlights of the tour may include the recently renovated Winnipeg Jets and Manitoba Moose dressing rooms, the player benches, press box, Matt Frost Media Centre, Manitoba Liquor & Lotteries Premium Suite Concourse, PlayNow Lounge, and more. Access varies by tour based on venue activity, and guests are encouraged to visit canadalifecentre.ca/tours for complete info. “We’re excited to open the doors and give people a look behind the scenes of a bustling sports and entertainment venue, including our newly renovated home team complex, which is one of the most state-of-the-art hockey ops spaces in the NHL,” said Kyle Phillips, Sr. Director of Guest Experience with True North Sports + Entertainment. “Whether during or outside of hockey season, fans and visitors from near and far can experience something uniquely Winnipeg on these tours and see what makes Canada Life Centre such an important part of our downtown story.” Winnipeg Jets and Manitoba Moose Season Ticket Members can purchase tickets now for November and early December tours on Ticketmaster , with tickets for the general public on sale Friday, Nov. 27 at 10 a.m. Tickets are $25 plus the $5 Ticketmaster order fee with discounts available for Jets and Moose Season Ticket Members and groups of 10 or more. The tour schedule is built around Canada Life Centre’s event calendar, and schedules will be released monthly. For schedules, FAQs and to book, visit canadalifecentre.ca/tours . records.excerpt: Title: As Pentagon blasts Canada's defence spending, Carney says Trump hasn't raised concerns URL Source: http://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/carney-trump-pentagon-criticism-canada-defence-spending-military-readiness-9.7435718 Final URL: https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/carney-trump-pentagon-criticism-canada-defence-spending-military-readiness-9.7435718 Published Time: 2026-11-25T17:42:23.489Z Markdown Content: [Politics](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics) Prime Minister Mark Carney said U.S. President Donald Trump hasn't raised issues with him about Canada not pulling its weight defending North America, despite the Pentagon blasting Canada about it. ## Pentagon threatening to look at more significant measures [Ashley Burke](https://www.cbc.ca/news/author/ashley-burke-1.2943844) · CBC News · Posted: Nov 25, 2026 10:42 AM PDT | Last Updated: November 25 ![Image 1: Text to Speech Icon](https://www.cbc.ca/a/assets/texttospeech.svg) Listen to this article Estimated 4 minutes The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. ![Image 2: A man in a suit standing in the House of Commons and pointing his finger.](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/0c8f91ae-37d5-4c62-8e32-eb4a5aa9b15e,1795640263626/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C318%2C4901%2C2756%29%3B) Prime Minister Mark Carney rises during Question Period on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026.(Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press) Prime Minister Mark Carney said U.S. President Donald Trump hasn't raised issues with him about Canada not pulling its weight defending North America, despite the Pentagon blasting Canada about it. Pete Hegseth's Department of War took aim at Canada this week saying it [isn't meeting its international obligations to NORAD or NATO](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/pentagon-criticizes-canadian-military-readiness-9.7433335) and is prioritizing its economic interests, which is hurting their joint force and American taxpayers. The Pentagon issued [a new threat on Tuesday,](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/defence-canada-us-pentagon-spending-9.7434887) saying it would look into more significant measures if it doesn't get what it wants from Canada. "Look, the commander-in-chief of the U.S. military is the president of the United States. And I can assure you that in my discussions with the president of the United States, we're focused on conflict resolution around the world," Carney said. "And he has not raised issues such as has been reported recently." * [Exclusive NATO's No. 2 commander strikes different tone on Canada than Pentagon](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/defence-spending-pentagon-nato-carney-9.7435919) Senior Pentagon official Elbridge Colby said last week at NATO headquarters he wanted "to see more from Canada" to meet its requirements for NORAD, the aerospace command jointly run by Canada and the U.S. Then news leaked on Friday that the U.S. military [now has restrictions interacting with Canadians](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/canada-us-pentagon-restrictions-hegseth-9.7431302). The Pentagon escalated its criticism of Canada on Monday by releasing a "fact sheet" taking aim at Canada's defence spending and saying the country is not a credible partner. _**WATCH | Carney says Trump 'has not raised' Canada's military investments:**_ ![Image 3](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/5c9d36eb-f610-4bce-baf8-ea393a536fb5,1795621394075/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C85%2C8273%2C4653%29%3BResize%3D620) Carney says Trump 'has not raised' Canada's military investments in conversations November 25| Duration 0:55 Asked about the Pentagon saying Canada isn't pulling its weight on North American defence, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his recent discussions with U.S. President Donald Trump have focused on 'conflict resolution around the world.' Carney responded for the first time on Wednesday, saying Canada is making "historic investments" in the military and defended the country's work with NATO. "Look, Canada is taking responsibility for our defence," Carney said. "We're at the front lines of NATO's defence, Operation Reassurance in Latvia. We're working with our NATO partners, including the United States, but very much with the Nordics, with Germany, with France, through the High North, the Arctic, in Europe, down through to the Baltics." Stephen Saideman, a defence expert at Carleton University, said what's really going on is that Hegseth is trying to "bully" Canada into dropping its plan to diversify defence spending to become less reliant on the U.S. Carney said last year that Canada is sending more than 75 cents of every dollar of capital spending on defence goes to the U.S. He called that "not smart" and promised to spend more at home. ## 'We'll make our own decisions' Asked by CBC News if the government will change that strategy after the Pentagon's latest threat, Secretary of State for Defence Procurement Stephen Fuhr suggested they wouldn't drop the diversification plan. "I think the minister of national defence made it very clear. We're a sovereign country. We'll make our own decisions," Fuhr said. _**WATCH | 'We'll make our own decisions,' Fuhr says:**_ ![Image 4](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/f192ffb9-b1c2-4e50-8c34-43ab30f15ec6,1795625546179/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C0%2C1920%2C1080%29%3BResize%3D620) 'We'll make our own decisions' on defence procurement, Fuhr says November 25| Duration 1:04 Asked about a senior Pentagon official's threat to look at 'significant mitigation measures' if Canada doesn't speed up its defence investments for North America, Secretary of State for Defence Procurement Stephen Fuhr said while Canada will continue to work with the U.S., 'we're a sovereign country.' Fuhr said he didn't have the calculations showing exactly how much defence spending in the U.S. has dropped, but said "there has been a noticeable shift." "We're continuing to buy from the U.S.," he said. "We're putting more effort into buying at home. We're putting more effort into partnering with other people." He pointed to Canada buying Boeing P-8 Poseidon surveillance aircraft and [HIMARS rocket launchers](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/army-artillery-defence-canada-us-9.7221033) as examples that they're still buying American. He said many other products contain U.S. components. * [Pentagon prepared to 'up the ante' in defence dispute with Canada](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/defence-canada-us-pentagon-spending-9.7434887) "So the U.S. is still getting a little piece of pretty much everything we do," he said. He said Canada "makes good stuff here" and needs to stimulate its own economy. Asked what his message is to Hegseth, Fuhr said "he should maybe get a current update on what Canada is doing, so he can see the effort and speed at which we're moving — because it's fast." _**WATCH | Hegseth shouldn't be dictating Canada's defence policy, Poilievre says:**_ ![Image 5](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/9ad5db9c-9c0e-4525-9cd0-0f6a4e5bafed,1795641546997/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C100%2C4480%2C2520%29%3BResize%3D620) Hegseth shouldn't be dictating Canada's defence policy, Poilievre says November 25| Duration 1:12 As the Pentagon drags Canada's defence spending and military readiness, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said 'we can simultaneously say' that U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth 'shouldn't be dictating our policy here at home while saying that the Liberals are failing to deliver on their own promises.' Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he's concerned that although billions of dollars are flowing, the money isn't reaching the men and women in uniform. "Two things can be true at once. We can simultaneously say that the U.S. defence secretary shouldn't be dictating our policy here at home, while saying that the Liberals are failing to deliver on their own promises," he said. ## ABOUT THE AUTHOR Ashley Bu

records.title: Canada can help strengthen democracy in the Western Balkans
records.excerpt: Canada can help strengthen democracy in the Western Balkans Skip to content Policy Options fr fr Commentary Canada can help strengthen democracy in the Western Balkans Ottawa can post more diplomats to the region, target corruption and fund the local groups that keep watch over elections and public spending. November 27, 2026 by Azra Dizdarevic Supporters of the opposition Student List gather to celebrate its victory in the 2026 Serbian parliamentary election at the House of the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, in Nikola Pasic Square. (Alexander Ryumin/TASS via ZUMA Press) Share Linkedin Icon-bluesky-icon Envelope Print X-twitter As the federal government increasingly anchors its strategic and geopolitical future to the European Union, its engagement in the Western Balkans should extend beyond regional crisis management to supporting the democratic values and civic engagement that shape its future. For decades, the Western Balkan nations – Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Serbia – have been trying to get into the European Union. However, they continue to face difficult hurdles related to unresolved territorial disputes between them and strict EU enlargement rules that demand greater judicial independence and anti-corruption measures, media freedom and democratic governance. The new Canada-EU alliance for the future offers Ottawa an opportunity to help. The Canada-EU summit statement (Part 8) in October calls on both parties to “sharpen our focus on shared priorities,” including the Western Balkans, among other regions. There are three key steps that Ottawa can take: strengthen its diplomatic engagement with the region; impose sanctions against officials implicated in significant corruption or similar conduct; and better target its financial contributions to the region. Serbia’s students change the political picture Serbia’s parliamentary elections in October add another reason for Canada to pay attention. For more than a decade, Western nations pursued a flawed strategy of transactional appeasement with Belgrade, treating its entrenched leadership as an anchor for regional stability while looking away from a corrosive decline in domestic democracy. But that stability proved brittle. A two-year, student-led protest movement, launched after a railway station canopy collapse that killed 16 people, resulted in a student-backed slate of academics, experts and other professionals winning 140 of 250 seats and forming the new government . While the long-term trajectory of Belgrade’s foreign policies under the new government is yet to be seen, including its path toward the EU, the election proved that genuine civic action can still alter the political landscape. The Western Balkans countries are moving at different speeds toward EU integration. The European Commission’s November 2026 enlargement reports describe increasing disengagement from the EU path in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the absence of a functioning ruling coalition has stalled key reforms. Divisive actors are hollowing out governance while close aides of U.S. President Donald Trump back a secessionist-leaning administration in the autonomous region of Republika Srpska. Serbia made no substantive progress in accession negotiations in the last year, as the commission noted “persistent political polarization” and negative trends in the judiciary and fundamental rights. On the other hand, Montenegro inched closer to joining the EU . Albania, also a frontrunner, faces domestic unrest , while North Macedonia is in persistent political friction . Meanwhile, according to the latest European Commission Western Balkans analysis , Kosovo remains at the earliest stage as a potential candidate, stalled by domestic institutional crises and a lack of formal recognition from five EU member states. Canada’s stake in the region These are European concerns, but they also affect the Euro-Atlantic security architecture in which Canada is invested. During a June hearing of the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee, witnesses described Russian interference (p.14, 16-17) in the region, including cyberattacks, disinformation and financial backing for pro-Russian parties. Jasmin Mujanović , a political scientist and policy expert on the region, told the committee the Western Balkans had fallen off the Western foreign policy agenda, allowing Russia and China (p.11) to build influence while leaving Canada behind in energy projects across Southeastern Europe. Canada already has a substantial presence in the region, with some 40,000 Canadian Forces personnel having served in the former Yugoslavia. Canada’s military mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina lasted almost 19 years, ending in March 2010. Canada also remains on the steering board of the Peace Implementation Council and has invested more than $540 million in development projects in the region since 1995, with Bosnia and Herzegovina being one of the largest recipients. Brussels and Ottawa have committed to defining by 2027 the concept of an “ever-closer association” short of full EU membership. While details are still to be worked out, the joint statement envisages regular summits and ministerial exchanges. The October summit statement also commits both sides to developing a framework for co-operation on democratic resilience, including electoral integrity, information space integrity and early-warning mechanisms. Canada and the EU should work together to ensure this applies to the Western Balkans, too. What Ottawa can do First, Ottawa should strengthen its diplomatic engagement with the region by expanding the dedicated capacity of its embassy in Budapest, which is currently accredited to Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the June parliamentary hearing (p.13) , Mujanović argued the lack of sustained Canadian representation makes substantive engagement difficult. While opening physical embassies in each country is unrealistic under current fiscal constraints, Canada can bridge this gap by reinforcing the existing hub-and-spoke model. By deploying roving diplomatic staff out of the Budapest hub, scaling up senior-level visits and introducing a centralized co-ordinator role to synchronize efforts with Canada’s embassy in Belgrade, Ottawa can achieve consistent, meaningful engagement with local institutions, civil society and independent media. Second, Canada should consider targeted measures under its sanctions legislation against officials implicated in significant corruption or conduct that amounts to a grave breach of international peace and security. How Canada could get much closer to Europe Canada’s industrial ambitions depend on stronger communities Canada-EU trade and diversification Canada failed to heed the warning signs of key U.S. policy For example, at the June hearing, Conservative MP Lianne Rood noted Canada had no sanctions against anyone undermining Bosnia’s Dayton Peace Agreement at that point, most notably Milorad Dodik, de facto strongman of Republika Srpska, Bosnia’s Serb-dominated entity, who has faced international scrutiny for unconstitutional acts and separatist rhetoric. Finally, Canada’s financial contribution can be more targeted. Building on the Canada Fund for Local Initiatives – which supports projects designed by local partners and lists democratic governance, the rule of law and human rights among its priorities – Ottawa could prioritize funding in the region for independent media, anti-corruption organizations, and civic groups monitoring public spending and electoral integrity. The EU commission has also presented a framework for gradual integration of the Western Balkan nations in energy, transport, digital and defence. As opportunities under this framework are developed, Canada should use its new EU channels to advocate for transparent procurement, credible environmental review and local consultation in such initiatives. Canada should not seek to manage the Western Balkan’s political future. H

records.title: AI Data Center Memory Demand Reshapes U.S. Smartphone Market, Lifting Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) While Crushing Budget Rivals
records.excerpt: Surging memory costs driven by artificial intelligence data center demand have upended the U.S. smartphone industry, punishing budget-focused manufacturers Surging memory costs driven by artificial intelligence data center demand have upended the U.S. smartphone industry, punishing budget-focused manufacturers and handing Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) a decisive competitive advantage. Overall U.S. smartphone shipments dropped 9% year over year in the third quarter, with Apple standing alone among major manufacturers in avoiding a volume decline, according to Counterpoint Research. The memory cost squeeze hits hardest at the lower end of the market, where razor-thin margins leave manufacturers with almost no buffer to absorb rising component prices. Motorola suffered the steepest fallout, watching its share of U.S. shipments collapse to 8% from 12% a year prior, a direct consequence of its budget-heavy product lineup’s vulnerability to component inflation. Google (NASDAQ: GOOG) also lost ground, with its U.S. shipment share slipping to 6% from 7%, even as the company launched its Pixel 11 flagship to try to maintain momentum. The Pixel 11 debuted at $899, a full $100 higher than its predecessor’s starting price, though Google did double the device’s storage capacity to soften the blow for buyers. Apple raised U.S. prices by $100 across the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max, and older models it continues to sell, though the increase on new models came in below what several analysts had anticipated. The company’s enormous scale gives it meaningful negotiating leverage with memory suppliers, a structural advantage that budget Android makers simply cannot replicate given their margin constraints. Apple’s share of U.S. smartphone shipments climbed to 57% in the third quarter, up sharply from 50% during the same period last year, consolidating its dominance at a time when rivals are retreating. Smartphone sales across the three largest U.S. carriers fell 4% year over year in the quarter, and Counterpoint sees no relief arriving during what is traditionally the industry’s strongest selling season. The research firm expects carriers to become more selective with promotional offers this holiday period, reducing the deal-driven volume that has historically buoyed fourth-quarter numbers. Counterpoint senior analyst Maurice Klaehne captured the shift in consumer behavior bluntly, saying “Consumers are timing their purchases around the best deals more than ever, if they buy at all.” Klaehne added that “This year’s holiday sales cycle will look quite different from usual,” a warning that underscores how deeply the memory crunch is reshaping purchasing patterns across the entire market. With AI infrastructure investment showing no signs of cooling, the upward pressure on memory prices is not expected to ease, leaving budget Android manufacturers facing a prolonged period of margin compression and market share erosion.
